section_summary: This section opens with a June 23, 1949 memorandum weighing seven ways to reach or defer a Japanese peace settlement, including negotiations with or without the Soviet Union, bilateral treaties, continued occupation, and a congressional resolution. A second study compares indefinite occupation with a peace treaty and favors a settlement that would restore Japanese independence while allowing security agreements. The final pages introduce reports on police action during labor demonstrations at the Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly on May 30–31, 1949.

subfiles.title: Possible procedures for a Japanese peace settlement
subfiles.about: Assesses whether and how the United States should pursue a peace settlement with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum compares negotiations through the Council of Foreign Ministers or Far Eastern Commission, negotiations excluding the Soviet Union and possibly China, referral to the United Nations, parallel bilateral treaties, continued occupation, and a congressional resolution ending the state of war. It examines voting rights, legal authority, territorial questions, reparations, occupation controls, and U.S. security needs. It also considers a separate U.S.–Japan bases agreement after a general settlement.

subfiles.title: Cover note: Advantages and Disadvantages of Indefinitely Continued Occupation or Conclusion of a Peace Settlement
subfiles.about: Introduces a preliminary study of occupation, a peace treaty, and accompanying Pacific security agreements.
subfiles.summary: Calls the attached section preliminary and explains its proposed security agreements.

subfiles.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Indefinitely Continued Occupation or Conclusion of a Peace Settlement
subfiles.about: Compares indefinite U.S. occupation with a peace settlement restoring Japanese independence.
subfiles.summary: The study weighs continued U.S. control and aid against Japanese resentment, limited autonomy, and the lack of international recognition under indefinite occupation. It proposes a brief treaty, territorial and property provisions, an end to post-treaty controls, and room for Japanese defense forces and security agreements. It concludes that a settlement would better secure a Japan aligned with the United States.

subfiles.title: Tokyo’s 450 of July 11, 1949
subfiles.about: Comments on a Tokyo despatch addressing Soviet allegations of police brutality at May 1949 demonstrations.
subfiles.summary: Says witnesses found no police brutality and urges continued reporting on incidents likely to prompt Soviet charges.

subfiles.title: Police Action in Labor Demonstrations of May 30–31, 1949
subfiles.from: Clyde K. Huston, U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese police reports and an investigation of Kinji Hashimoto’s death during Tokyo labor demonstrations.
subfiles.summary: Reports that prosecutors considered Hashimoto’s death accidental and that U.S. police specialists saw no unnecessary force.

subfiles.title: MPD Daily Report: Filibuster at Metropolitan Assembly
subfiles.from: Director, Guard and Traffic Section, Tokyo Metropolitan Police
subfiles.about: Records police deployment and events around the May 30–31 demonstration at the Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly.
subfiles.summary: The report describes protesters entering and gathering around the Assembly, orders to disperse, police reinforcements, and the crowd’s departure after midnight. It also records the death of a streetcar conductor and injuries to police and others. The report continues beyond page 67.
